chunks.text: What if your future home becomes cheaper
but your retirement becomes more expensive
What if companies desperately need workers
but hospitals cannot find enough nurses
And what if governments offer people money
to have babies
but the next generation still gets smaller
This might sound like the beginning of
a science-fiction movie
But the demographic shift behind it is
already happening
According to the United Nations' World Fertility
2024 report
fertility was below replacement level in 55 percent
of the world's countries and areas
That does not mean humanity is about
to disappear
It means something more complicated
many societies are moving toward a future
with fewer young people and a larger
share of older adults
So
what happens when an economy built around
each generation being bigger meets a generation
that is smaller
Let's explore five possible futures
First we need to understand one number
In countries with low mortality
around 2.1 children per woman is the
fertility level needed for one generation to
replace itself over the long term
without migration
It is a population average not a
target for every family

segs.kick: FERTILITY RATE IS NOT BIRTHS THIS YEAR

chunks.text: And the fertility rate is not the
same as the number of babies born
this year
It estimates how many children a woman
would have if current age-specific birth rates
continued throughout her reproductive life
Now imagine 100 couples
In a simplified example
if every couple has two children
they have 200 children altogether
If those couples average just one child
the next generation has only 100
If that pattern continues the following generation
could be smaller again
Real populations are more complicated
People live longer
move between countries and have children at
different ages
A country can even keep growing for
years after fertility falls below replacement
But over decades smaller birth cohorts change
the shape of society
And that brings us to our first
scenario

params.title: WHAT IF THERE ARE FEWER WORKERS?

chunks.text: Imagine a town twenty-five years from now
Its largest generation is retiring
But the generation entering work is much
smaller
The local supermarket needs staff
Construction companies need electricians
The hospital needs carers
At first that could be good news
for some workers
Employers may offer higher wages better training
or more flexible hours because people are
harder to recruit
But now imagine you own a small
bakery
You raise wages to attract staff
Your supplier has done the same
So has the delivery company
Your costs increase
You might raise prices shorten opening hours
buy equipment
or close
That does not mean every labour shortage
creates inflation
or that every business loses
Demand changes too
Fewer children could mean less demand for
some school supplies
while an older population needs more healthcare
The challenge is matching the workers we
have with the services people need
And here is the crucial distinction
A smaller economy is not automatically a
poorer society
If fewer workers produce more value per
person
living standards can still improve
Which takes us to the biggest financial
question
Imagine a shared dinner
Ten people contribute money to feed themselves
and a few relatives
Over time
several contributors retire
Now fewer people are earning
while more people still need dinner
Many public pension systems face a version
of this problem
today's workers help finance today's retirees
As populations age governments may face difficult
choices
Increase contributions
Raise taxes
Adjust benefits
Encourage longer working lives
Or move money away from other priorities
But pensions are not identical everywhere
Some rely more on taxes some on
contributions and others include substantial invested savings
An ageing population does not automatically mean
your pension disappears
It means the system may need to
change
Now consider two people asked to work
longer
One has a flexible office job
The other has spent forty years lifting
heavy materials
The same retirement age can affect them
very differently

segs.kick: WHO? UNDER WHAT CONDITIONS? WITH WHAT SUPPORT?

chunks.text: So the question is not simply
Can people work longer
It is Who can work longer under
what conditions and with what support
And remember
longer lives are an achievement
The problem is failing to adapt our
institutions to them
Here is the scenario many younger viewers
might welcome
Fewer people
More empty homes
Lower prices

segs.kick: POSSIBLE IN SOME PLACES. NOT GUARANTEED.

chunks.text: Possible
Yes in some places
Guaranteed everywhere
Absolutely not
Imagine two locations in the same country
A small town loses younger residents
Its school closes
Shops struggle
Housing demand weakens
Meanwhile the capital city keeps attracting students
migrants and workers
Housing there can remain expensive
even while the national population shrinks
There is another twist
Homes are occupied by households not by
population totals
If more people live alone
a country can need more homes even
without adding more people
Older residents may also need different housing
smaller properties accessible entrances and locations close
to healthcare
So demographic change could create an unusual
future
Empty houses in places where jobs have
disappeared
and housing shortages where people still need
to live
A cheap house is much less useful
if the nearest employer hospital or supermarket
is far away

params.title: WHAT IF AI FILLS THE GAP?

chunks.text: Now imagine a different response
Instead of trying to replace every missing
worker
we help each worker accomplish more
Software reduces paperwork
Machines handle repetitive factory tasks
Better equipment allows older workers to remain
employed comfortably
In a simplified example
if a team becomes ten percent smaller
but each remaining worker becomes productive enough
total output could be maintained
That is why productivity matters so much
But
AI will fix it skips several difficult
steps
Technology costs money
Businesses need time to adopt it
Workers need training
And the benefits may not reach everyone
equally
Most importantly producing more digital content is
different from helping someone shower
repairing a water pipe
or comforting a frightened patient
Some tasks are much harder to automate
than others
So imagine two futures
In one
technology helps a smaller workforce support a
good quality of life
In the other productivity gains concentrate in
a few companies while essential services remain
understaffed
The technology matters
How we use it matters just as
much

params.title: WHAT IF GOVERNMENTS TRY TO REVERSE IT?

chunks.text: Suppose a government announces a baby bonus
Will births suddenly return to replacement level
There is no guaranteed result

items: Can we afford a suitable home?
Can we balance work and family?
Do we want to be parents?

chunks.text: Because deciding to have a child involves
much more than one payment
Can we afford a suitable home
Is childcare available
Will we lose income
Can we balance work and family life
Do we actually want to become parents
Some people want fewer children
Others want children but face barriers
Those are different situations and policy needs
to recognise that
Affordable childcare parental leave stable employment
and housing can make family life easier
But even if births increase tomorrow
those babies will not become nurses or
taxpayers next year
They need roughly two decades to enter
the workforce
What about immigration
It can bring working-age people into a
country much sooner
But successful migration also requires housing
infrastructure
fair working conditions and ways to recognise
people's skills
And migration moves people between countries
It does not increase the global population
It can be part of the response
alongside training productivity and better opportunities for
people already living there
There is no single switch that fixes
demographic change
But here is the twist
A smaller future generation does not automatically
mean a worse future
It could mean fewer pressures on some
resources more investment per child
and stronger incentives to improve productivity
It could also mean stretched care services
struggling communities and difficult financial choices
Both outcomes are possible
What matters is the pace of change
and whether societies prepare
The world is not following one demographic
path
Some populations are still growing rapidly
while others are ageing and shrinking
So the challenge is not simply getting
everyone to have more babies
It is building a society where people
can make real choices about family life
and where a good standard of living
does not depend entirely on having more
people every generation
Because the biggest question is not
What if there are fewer of us
It is
What if our systems never learn how
to adapt
If your country's next generation were smaller
what would you change first
housing retirement
or the way we work
Tell us in the comments
